base_method_text.title: FiT: Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion Model
base_method_text.summary:
Nature is infinitely resolution-free. In the context of this reality,
existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face
challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain.
To overcome this limitation, we present the Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT),
a transformer architecture specifically designed for generating images with
unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios. Unlike traditional methods that
perceive images as static-resolution grids, FiT conceptualizes images as
sequences of dynamically-sized tokens. This perspective enables a flexible
training strategy that effortlessly adapts to diverse aspect ratios during both
training and inference phases, thus promoting resolution generalization and
eliminating biases induced by image cropping. Enhanced by a meticulously
adjusted network structure and the integration of training-free extrapolation
techniques, FiT exhibits remarkable flexibility in resolution extrapolation
generation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance
of FiT across a broad range of resolutions, showcasing its effectiveness both
within and beyond its training resolution distribution. Repository available at
https://github.com/whlzy/FiT.
base_method_text.main_contributions: The paper introduces Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT), a novel transformer architecture for diffusion models that generates images at arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios. FiT overcomes the resolution limitations of existing Diffusion Transformers by conceptualizing images as sequences of dynamically-sized tokens, enabling flexible training and resolution extrapolation. The paper presents a flexible training pipeline, a unique transformer architecture for dynamic token length modeling, and a training-free resolution extrapolation method.
base_method_text.methodology: FiT builds upon the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture and incorporates 2D Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), Swish-Gated Linear Unit (SwiGLU), and Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA). It employs a flexible training pipeline that preserves the original image aspect ratio and pads token sequences to a maximum length. Training-free resolution extrapolation techniques, including VisionNTK and VisionYaRN, are adapted for 2D RoPE to enhance performance across various resolutions.
base_method_text.experimental_setup: The model was trained on the ImageNet dataset with a maximum resolution limit of HW ⩽ 256^2. The experiments benchmark class-conditional image generation at various resolutions (160×320, 128×384, 320×320, 224×448, and 160×480) and aspect ratios (1:1, 1:2, 1:3). Evaluation metrics include Fre'chet Inception Distance (FID), sFID, Inception Score (IS), Precision, and Recall. Both in-distribution and out-of-distribution resolutions were used for evaluation.
base_method_text.limitations: The FiT-XL/2 model was trained for a limited number of steps (1.8M), resulting in slightly inferior performance at 256x256 resolution compared to DiT-XL/2. The generative capabilities of FiT-XL/2 with higher resolution training (larger token length limitation) have not been thoroughly explored. The research primarily focuses on training-free resolution extrapolation techniques, without delving into methods requiring additional training.
base_method_text.future_research_directions: Future research could explore training FiT with higher resolutions and larger token lengths. Investigating resolution extrapolation methods that require additional training could further enhance the model's capabilities. Additionally, exploring different architectural modifications and their impact on flexible image synthesis would be a valuable avenue for future work.

add_method_texts.title:
FiTv2: Scalable and Improved Flexible Vision Transformer for Diffusion
  Model
add_method_texts.summary:
\textit{Nature is infinitely resolution-free}. In the context of this
reality, existing diffusion models, such as Diffusion Transformers, often face
challenges when processing image resolutions outside of their trained domain.
To address this limitation, we conceptualize images as sequences of tokens with
dynamic sizes, rather than traditional methods that perceive images as
fixed-resolution grids. This perspective enables a flexible training strategy
that seamlessly accommodates various aspect ratios during both training and
inference, thus promoting resolution generalization and eliminating biases
introduced by image cropping. On this basis, we present the \textbf{Flexible
Vision Transformer} (FiT), a transformer architecture specifically designed for
generating images with \textit{unrestricted resolutions and aspect ratios}. We
further upgrade the FiT to FiTv2 with several innovative designs, includingthe
Query-Key vector normalization, the AdaLN-LoRA module, a rectified flow
scheduler, and a Logit-Normal sampler. Enhanced by a meticulously adjusted
network structure, FiTv2 exhibits $2\times$ convergence speed of FiT. When
incorporating advanced training-free extrapolation techniques, FiTv2
demonstrates remarkable adaptability in both resolution extrapolation and
diverse resolution generation. Additionally, our exploration of the scalability
of the FiTv2 model reveals that larger models exhibit better computational
efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce an efficient post-training strategy to
adapt a pre-trained model for the high-resolution generation. Comprehensive
experiments demonstrate the exceptional performance of FiTv2 across a broad
range of resolutions. We have released all the codes and models at
\url{https://github.com/whlzy/FiT} to promote the exploration of diffusion
transformer models for arbitrary-resolution image generation.
add_method_texts.main_contributions: The paper introduces FiTv2, an enhanced version of the Flexible Vision Transformer (FiT), designed for generating images with arbitrary resolutions and aspect ratios. FiTv2 incorporates innovations like Query-Key Vector Normalization, AdaLN-LoRA, a rectified flow scheduler, and a Logit-Normal sampler, achieving faster convergence and improved scalability compared to FiT. It also presents a mixed data preprocessing strategy and demonstrates exceptional performance across a broad range of resolutions and text-to-image tasks.
add_method_texts.methodology: FiTv2 builds upon the DiT architecture and incorporates 2-D Rotary Positional Embedding (2-D RoPE), Swish-Gated Linear Units (SwiGLU), and Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention. It uses a flexible training pipeline that treats images as token sequences and employs rectified flow for faster convergence. The model also uses a Logit-Normal sampler for timestep selection and incorporates training-free extrapolation techniques for resolution generalization.
add_method_texts.experimental_setup: The model was trained and evaluated on the ImageNet dataset with various resolutions and aspect ratios. Performance was measured using metrics like Fre'chet Inception Distance (FID), sFID, Inception Score (IS), and improved Precision and Recall. The effectiveness of FiTv2 was validated through class-guided image generation and text-to-image generation tasks, comparing it against state-of-the-art CNN and transformer models.
add_method_texts.limitations: The original FiT architecture had limitations including underperformance on the standard ImageNet 256x256 benchmark and increased parameter count and computational costs compared to DiT. While FiTv2 addresses some of these, specific limitations of FiTv2 itself are not explicitly stated in the provided text. The reliance on a pre-trained VAE might also introduce constraints.
add_method_texts.future_research_directions: Future research directions include exploring the scalability of FiTv2 further, investigating the transfer learning capabilities from low to high resolution, and designing more powerful diffusion transformer models. Further investigation into improved training-free resolution extrapolation methods could also be beneficial.

```python
class FiT(nn.Module):
    """
    Flexible Diffusion model with a Transformer backbone.
    """
    def __init__(
        self,
        context_size: int = 256,
        patch_size: int = 2,
        in_channels: int = 4,
        hidden_size: int = 1152,
        depth: int = 28,
        num_heads: int = 16,
        mlp_ratio: float = 4.0,
        class_dropout_prob: float = 0.1,
        num_classes: int = 1000,
        learn_sigma: bool = True,
        use_sit: bool = False,
        use_checkpoint: bool=False,
        use_swiglu: bool = False,
        use_swiglu_large: bool = False,
        rel_pos_embed: Optional[str] = 'rope',
        norm_type: str = "layernorm",
        q_norm: Optional[str] = None,
        k_norm: Optional[str] = None,
        qk_norm_weight: bool = False,
        qkv_bias: bool = True,
        ffn_bias: bool = True,
        adaln_bias: bool = True,
        adaln_type: str = "normal",
        adaln_lora_dim: int = None,
        rope_theta: float = 10000.0,
        custom_freqs: str = 'normal',
        max_pe_len_h: Optional[int] = None,
        max_pe_len_w: Optional[int] = None,
        decouple: bool = False,
        ori_max_pe_len: Optional[int] = None,
        online_rope: bool = False,
        add_rel_pe_to_v: bool = False,
        pretrained_ckpt: str = None,
        ignore_keys: list = None,
        finetune: str = None,
        time_shifting: int = 1,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.context_size = context_size
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        assert not (learn_sigma and use_sit)
        self.learn_sigma = learn_sigma
        self.use_sit = use_sit
        self.use_checkpoint = use_checkpoint
        self.depth = depth
        self.mlp_ratio = mlp_ratio
        self.class_dropout_prob = class_dropout_prob
        self.num_classes = num_classes
        self.in_channels = in_channels
        self.out_channels = self.in_channels * 2 if learn_sigma else in_channels
        self.patch_size = patch_size
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.adaln_type = adaln_type
        self.online_rope = online_rope
        self.time_shifting = time_shifting

        self.x_embedder = PatchEmbedder(in_channels * patch_size**2, hidden_size, bias=True)
        self.t_embedder = TimestepEmbedder(hidden_size)
        self.y_embedder = LabelEmbedder(num_classes, hidden_size, class_dropout_prob)
        
        self.rel_pos_embed = VisionRotaryEmbedding(
            head_dim=hidden_size//num_heads, theta=rope_theta, custom_freqs=custom_freqs, online_rope=online_rope,
            max_pe_len_h=max_pe_len_h, max_pe_len_w=max_pe_len_w, decouple=decouple, ori_max_pe_len=ori_max_pe_len,
        )
        
        if adaln_type == 'lora':
            self.global_adaLNm_modulation = nn.Sequential(
                nn.SiLU(),
                nn.Linear(hidden_size, 6 * hidden_size, bias=adaln_bias)
            )
        else:
            self.global_adaLNm_modulation = None        
        
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([FiTBlock(
            hidden_size, num_heads, mlp_ratio=mlp_ratio, swiglu=use_swiglu, swiglu_large=use_swiglu_large,
            rel_pos_embed=rel_pos_embed, add_rel_pe_to_v=add_rel_pe_to_v, norm_layer=norm_type, 
            q_norm=q_norm, k_norm=k_norm, qk_norm_weight=qk_norm_weight, qkv_bias=qkv_bias, ffn_bias=ffn_bias, 
            adaln_bias=adaln_bias, adaln_type=adaln_type, adaln_lora_dim=adaln_lora_dim
        ) for _ in range(depth)])
        self.final_layer = FinalLayer(hidden_size, patch_size, self.out_channels, norm_layer=norm_type, adaln_bias=adaln_bias, adaln_type=adaln_type)
        self.initialialize_weights(pretrained_ckpt=pretrained_ckpt, ignore=ignore_keys)
        if finetune != None:
            self.finetune(type=finetune, unfreeze=ignore_keys)

    def unpatchify(self, x, hw):
        """
        Args:
            x: (B, p**2 * C_out, N)
            N = H/p * W/p
        return:
            imgs: (B, C_out, H, W)
        """
        h, w = hw
        p = self.patch_size
        if self.use_sit:
            x = rearrange(x, "b (h w) c -> b h w c", h=h//p, w=w//p) # (B, h//2, w//2, 16) -> (B, h//2 * w//2, 16)
            x = rearrange(x, "b h w (c p1 p2) -> b c (h p1) (w p2)", p1=p, p2=p) # (B, h//2, w//2, 16) -> (B, h, w, 4)
        else:
            x = rearrange(x, "b c (h w) -> b c h w", h=h//p, w=w//p) # (B, 16, h//2 * w//2) -> (B, 16, h//2, w//2)
            x = rearrange(x, "b (c p1 p2) h w -> b c (h p1) (w p2)", p1=p, p2=p) # (B, 16, h//2, w//2) -> (B, 4, h, w)
        return x

    def forward(self, x, t, y, grid, mask, size=None):
        """
        Forward pass of FiT.
        x: (B, p**2 * C_in, N), tensor of sequential inputs (flattened latent features of images, N=H*W//(p**2))
        t: (B,), tensor of diffusion timesteps
        y: (B,), tensor of class labels
        grid: (B, 2, N), tensor of height and weight indices that spans a grid
        mask: (B, N), tensor of the mask for the sequence
        size: (B, n, 2), tensor of the height and width, n is the number of the packed iamges
        --------
        return: (B, p**2 * C_out, N), where C_out=2*C_in if leran_sigma, C_out=C_in otherwise.
        """
        
        t = torch.clamp(self.time_shifting * t / (1 + (self.time_shifting - 1) * t), max=1.0)        
        t = t.float().to(x.dtype)
        if not self.use_sit:
            x = rearrange(x, 'B C N -> B N C')            # (B, C, N) -> (B, N, C), where C = p**2 * C_in
        x = self.x_embedder(x)                      # (B, N, C) -> (B, N, D)  
        t = self.t_embedder(t)                      # (B, D)
        y = self.y_embedder(y, self.training)            # (B, D)
        c = t + y                                   # (B, D)
        
        # get RoPE freqs in advance, then calculate attention.
        if self.online_rope:            
            freqs_cos, freqs_sin = self.rel_pos_embed.online_get_2d_rope_from_grid(grid, size)
            freqs_cos, freqs_sin = freqs_cos.unsqueeze(1), freqs_sin.unsqueeze(1)
        else:
            freqs_cos, freqs_sin = self.rel_pos_embed.get_cached_2d_rope_from_grid(grid)
            freqs_cos, freqs_sin = freqs_cos.unsqueeze(1), freqs_sin.unsqueeze(1)
        if self.global_adaLNm_modulation != None:
            global_adaLNm = self.global_adaLNm_modulation(c)
        else: 
            global_adaLNm = 0.0
        
        if not self.use_checkpoint:
            for block in self.blocks:                              # (B, N, D)
                x = block(x, c, mask, freqs_cos, freqs_sin, global_adaLNm) 
        else:
            for block in self.blocks:
                x = torch.utils.checkpoint.checkpoint(self.ckpt_wrapper(block), x, c, mask, freqs_cos, freqs_sin, global_adaLNm)  

        x = self.final_layer(x, c)                         # (B, N, p**2 * C_out), where C_out=2*C_in if leran_sigma, C_out=C_in otherwise.
        x = x * mask[..., None]                                # mask the padding tokens
        if not self.use_sit:
            x = rearrange(x, 'B N C -> B C N')            # (B, N, C) -> (B, C, N), where C = p**2 * C_out
        return x
    
    def forward_with_cfg(self, x, t, y, grid, mask, size, cfg_scale, scale_pow=0.0):
        """
        Forward pass with classifier free guidance of FiT.
        x: (2B, N, p**2 * C_in) if use_sit else (2B, p**2 * C_in, N), tensor of sequential inputs (flattened latent features of images, N=H*W//(p**2))
        t: (2B,), tensor of diffusion timesteps
        y: (2B,), tensor of class labels
        grid: (2B, 2, N): tensor of height and weight indices that spans a grid
        mask: (2B, N): tensor of the mask for the sequence
        cfg_scale: float > 1.0
        return: (B, p**2 * C_out, N), where C_out=2*C_in if leran_sigma, C_out=C_in otherwise.
        """
        half = x[: len(x) // 2]                                     # (2B, ...) -> (B, ...)
        combined = torch.cat([half, half], dim=0)        # (2B, ...)
        model_out = self.forward(combined, t, y, grid, mask, size)   # (2B, N, C) if use_sit else (2B, C, N), where C = p**2 * C_out
        # For exact reprocudibility reasons, we apply classifier-free guidance on only
        # three channels by default. The standard approach to cfg applies it to all channels.
        # This can be done by uncommenting the following line and commenting-out the line
        # following that.
        # C_cfg = self.in_channels * self.patch_size * self.patch_size
        C_cfg = 3 * self.patch_size * self.patch_size
        if self.use_sit:
            eps, rest = model_out[:, :, :C_cfg], model_out[:, :, C_cfg:] # eps: (2B, N, C_cfg), where C_cfg = p**2 * 3
        else:
            eps, rest = model_out[:, :C_cfg], model_out[:, C_cfg:] # eps: (2B, C_cfg, N), where C_cfg = p**2 * 3
        cond_eps, uncond_eps = torch.split(eps, len(eps) // 2, dim=0)  # (2B, ...) -> (B, ...)
        # from https://github.com/sail-sg/MDT/blob/main/masked_diffusion/models.py#L506
        # improved classifier-free guidance
        if scale_pow == 0.0:
            real_cfg_scale = cfg_scale
        else:
            scale_step = (
                1-torch.cos(((1-torch.clamp_max(t, 1.0))*scale_pow)*torch.pi)
            )*1/2 # power-cos scaling 
            real_cfg_scale = (cfg_scale-1)*scale_step + 1
        t = t / (self.time_shifting + (1 - self.time_shifting) * t)
        half_eps = uncond_eps + real_cfg_scale * (cond_eps - uncond_eps)     # (B, ...)
        eps = torch.cat([half_eps, half_eps], dim=0)  # (B, ...) -> (2B, ...)
        if self.use_sit:
            return torch.cat([eps, rest], dim=2)      # (2B, N, C), where C = p**2 * C_out
        else:
            return torch.cat([eps, rest], dim=1)      # (2B, C, N), where C = p**2 * C_out
        
    def ckpt_wrapper(self, module):
        def ckpt_forward(*inputs):
            outputs = module(*inputs)
            return outputs
        return ckpt_forward
    
    @property
    def dtype(self) -> torch.dtype:
        """
        `torch.dtype`: The dtype of the module (assuming that all the module parameters have the same dtype).
        """
        return get_parameter_dtype(self)
    
    
    def finetune(self, type, unfreeze):
        if type == 'full':
            return
        for name, param in self.named_parameters():
            param.requires_grad = False

        for unf in unfreeze:
            for name, param in self.named_parameters():
                if unf in name: # LN means Layer Norm
                    param.requires_grad = True
```

new_method:
Below is an example of a new method derived from identifying key issues in the Base Method (FiT) and incorporating one of the novel approaches from the Add Method (FiTv2):

Proposed Method (Ultra-Scale Adaptive FiT, or “US-AFiT”)

1) Identified Issues in the Base Method (FiT):

• Limited Exploration of Very-High-Resolution Training: FiT’s dynamic token approach is flexible, but it has not been thoroughly explored for resolutions far beyond the 256² limit.  
• Underperformance at Standard Benchmarks: FiT-XL/2 trained for only 1.8M steps lags slightly behind DiT-XL/2 on the 256×256 ImageNet benchmark.  
• Exclusively Training-Free Extrapolation: FiT focuses on training-free resolution extrapolation and does not investigate techniques that leverage additional training steps for enhanced performance.

2) Selected Add Method Approach to Address an Issue:

• AdaLN-LoRA Module from FiTv2: This approach streamlines parameter-efficient fine-tuning and reduces training overhead. By injecting small LoRA networks into LayerNorm layers (through AdaLN), the model can be adaptively updated without large-scale parameter modifications, mitigating the limitations around resolution scaling.

3) A Truly New Method: “US-AFiT”

US-AFiT extends FiT by introducing a region-based training pipeline alongside AdaLN-LoRA:

• Region-Based Parallelization: Instead of merely padding tokens for flexible aspect ratios, US-AFiT subdivides ultra-high-resolution images into partially overlapping regions. Each region is treated as its own sequence of tokens, processed by the Transformer in parallel. A gated region-merging mechanism seamlessly blends the independently processed regions, preserving global coherence.  
• AdaLN-LoRA “Spot Fine-Tuning”: Inspired by FiTv2, US-AFiT integrates AdaLN-LoRA modules to selectively fine-tune the region-level attention and merging layers. This allows the model to adapt to large token counts without sacrificing performance, as only a small set of parameters needs to be updated for each region.  
• Hybrid Extrapolation and Incremental Training: US-AFiT merges FiT’s training-free extrapolation ideas with optional short “incremental training” cycles. When confronted with higher resolutions or new domains, the model can apply the AdaLN-LoRA modules to swiftly calibrate region-token embeddings. This preserves FiT’s plug-and-play extrapolation benefits while mitigating the underperformance at standardized benchmarks through targeted fine-tuning.

Together, these innovations allow US-AFiT to handle ultra-high resolutions more effectively, match or surpass state-of-the-art benchmarks with minimal overhead, and maintain flexibility across diverse image dimensions. By combining FiT’s dynamic token sequences with FiTv2’s AdaLN-LoRA modules (and adding region-level parallelization and optional fine-tuning), US-AFiT represents a fundamentally new approach beyond a simple partial modification.

Below is an experimental plan outlining three realistic and Python-implementable experiments designed to demonstrate the superiority of US-AFiT over the base FiT (and related methods):

──────────────────────────────
1. Region-Based Parallel Processing

• Objective:  
Validate that subdividing ultra-high-resolution images into overlapping regions—and processing them in parallel—improves both efficiency and accuracy in handling very high resolutions.

• Experiment Details:  
– Implement a pipeline (using PyTorch and libraries such as Torchvision) that splits high-resolution images (e.g., 1024×1024 or larger) into partially overlapping regions.  
– Process each region independently via a Transformer network, then use a gated region-merging module to reconstruct the full image prediction.  
– Compare the performance (e.g., image classification accuracy on high-res datasets and inference speed) with a baseline FiT implementation that processes the full image or uses simple padding/splitting without overlap.

• Metrics to Monitor:  
– Accuracy improvements on a high-resolution validation dataset.  
– Computational overhead and latency differences.  
– Qualitative assessments of boundary artifacts or merged-region coherence.

──────────────────────────────
2. AdaLN-LoRA “Spot Fine-Tuning” Module Efficiency

• Objective:  
Demonstrate that selectively fine-tuning only a small set of parameters via AdaLN-LoRA in region-level attention and merging layers can efficiently adapt the model to ultra-high-resolution inputs without a complete retraining.

• Experiment Details:  
– Integrate AdaLN-LoRA modules into the Transformer’s LayerNorm layers in your experimental US-AFiT model, ensuring only these “spot” modules are updated during fine-tuning.  
– Fine-tune the network on a subset of ultra-high-resolution images using limited incremental training steps.  
– In parallel, run a baseline where no additional fine-tuning is performed (i.e., the training-free extrapolation version) as well as one where the full network is fine-tuned lightly (as might be common in FiT).  
– Evaluate improvements in output quality (e.g., accuracy, image reconstruction quality, segmentation consistency, etc.) versus training overhead (parameters updated, training time).

• Metrics to Monitor:  
– Change in accuracy or loss before and after incremental fine-tuning.  
– Parameter efficiency (the number of parameters updated) and overall training time.  
– Improved adaptation to domain shifts between standard and ultra-high resolutions.

──────────────────────────────
3. Hybrid Extrapolation vs. Incremental Training Evaluation

• Objective:  
Assess the benefits of merging training-free resolution extrapolation with selective incremental training cycles, comparing performance across mixed resolutions and domains.

• Experiment Details:  
– Set up two training pipelines: one that only uses US-AFiT’s training-free extrapolation (using dynamic token scaling and region-based processing) and another that incorporates short incremental training cycles with AdaLN-LoRA based fine-tuning when switching to new domains or higher resolutions.  
– Simulate a domain shift scenario (e.g., training on one set of natural images and testing on a set with different resolution or characteristics) to see how well each pipeline adapts.  
– Implement these pipelines in Python using common deep-learning libraries such as PyTorch, possibly leveraging distributed training modules for region-based parallelization.

• Metrics to Monitor:  
– Performance differences on standard benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet for 256×256) versus ultra-high-resolution benchmarks.  
– Accuracy gains and robustness under domain shift.  
– The trade-off between computational overhead (additional fine-tuning cycles) and performance improvements.

──────────────────────────────
Implementation Considerations in Python:

– Utilize open-source frameworks (e.g., PyTorch) for model implementation, training, and evaluation.  
– Leverage data-loading tools (e.g., Torchvision’s datasets and transforms) to efficiently handle ultra-high-resolution images and custom region-splitting logic.  
– Incorporate logging (with tools like TensorBoard or Weights & Biases) to track metrics during training and evaluation.

──────────────────────────────
Outcome:

These experiments should demonstrate that US-AFiT:
• Achieves superior performance on very high-resolution tasks by efficiently processing overlapping regions.
• Benefits from the AdaLN-LoRA modules, which allow targeted fine-tuning without significant overhead.
• Maintains the flexible, training-free extrapolation benefits of FiT while strengthening performance via optional incremental training.

By coding these experiments in Python and leveraging existing deep learning frameworks, you are set up for a concrete demonstration of US-AFiT’s advantage over baseline methods.
experiment_details:
Below is one possible concrete experimental plan—with multiple independent (but complementary) experiments—that tests the US-AFiT advantages over the base FiT. In what follows, we describe three experiments using PyTorch, Torchvision, and other common libraries. Each experiment is described in detail, with its experimental objective, setup, code examples, evaluation metrics, and considerations for reproducibility.

──────────────────────────────
1. Experiment 1: Region‐Based Parallel Processing
──────────────────────────────
Objective:
• Validate that subdividing ultra‐high‐resolution images into overlapping regions—and processing them in parallel—improves both inference efficiency and prediction accuracy.  
• Assess whether the “gated region merging” module minimizes boundary artifacts when integrating the segmented outputs.

Experimental Setup:
• Data: Use a high-resolution dataset (for instance, a subset of ImageNet upscaled to 1024×1024 or larger).  
• Preprocessing: Write a custom function to split each image into overlapping regions (e.g., 256×256 patches with an overlap margin of 32 pixels).  
• Model:  
  – For each region, feed the region into a US-AFiT model (which builds on FiT but with region handling).  
  – To ensure parallel processing, use PyTorch’s DataLoader with multiple workers and Python’s ThreadPool or asynchronous execution (if needed).  
• Merger: Design a “gated region merging” module that accepts individual region outputs and uses learnable gates (or attention-based weighting) to combine overlapping predictions into a full-size output.  
• Baseline: Compare with a FiT implementation that either processes the full image at once (using padding/rescaling) or splits regions with no overlap.

# Standard python and pytorch libraries.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torchvision.transforms as T
from torchvision.datasets import ImageFolder
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import numpy as np

def split_image_regions(img, patch_size=256, overlap=32):
    """
    Split an image (Tensor CxHxW) into overlapping patches.

class GatedRegionMerger(nn.Module):
    """

class DummyPatchEmbedder(nn.Module):

class DummyTimestepEmbedder(nn.Module):

class DummyLabelEmbedder(nn.Module):

class DummyFiTBlock(nn.Module):

        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(int(hidden_size * mlp_ratio), hidden_size)
    def forward(self, x, c, mask, freqs_cos, freqs_sin, global_adaLNm):
        # a simple residual block with dummy computation
        out = self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))
        return x + out

class DummyFinalLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, hidden_size, patch_size, out_channels, **kwargs):

        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_size, patch_size * patch_size * out_channels)
        self.patch_size = patch_size
        self.out_channels = out_channels
    def forward(self, x, c):
        # simply project and reshape
        B, N, D = x.shape
        out = self.fc(x)  # (B, N, patch_size**2 * out_channels)
        return out

class FiT(nn.Module):
    """
    Dummy FiT model based on the research code.
    For demonstration, the forward method simply performs a few dummy linear transforms.
    """
    def __init__(self,
                 context_size: int = 256,
                 patch_size: int = 4,
                 in_channels: int = 3,
                 hidden_size: int = 128,
                 depth: int = 4,
                 num_heads: int = 4,
                 num_classes: int = 10,
                 adaln_type: str = "lora",
                 **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        self.context_size = context_size
        self.patch_size = patch_size
        self.in_channels = in_channels
        self.hidden_size = hidden_size
        self.num_heads = num_heads
        self.learn_sigma = False  # simplified for dummy
        self.depth = depth
        
        # Dummy components for embedding
        self.x_embedder = DummyPatchEmbedder(in_channels * patch_size * patch_size, hidden_size)
        self.t_embedder = DummyTimestepEmbedder(hidden_size)
        self.y_embedder = DummyLabelEmbedder(num_classes, hidden_size, dropout_prob=0.1)
        
        # Dummy blocks and final layer
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([DummyFiTBlock(hidden_size, num_heads) for _ in range(depth)])
        self.final_layer = DummyFinalLayer(hidden_size, patch_size, in_channels)
    
    def forward(self, x, t, y, grid, mask, size=None):
        # x is expected to be (B, C, H, W) (or flattened patches)
        B = x.shape[0]
        # flatten patches for embedding
        # assume x is (B, in_channels, patch_size, patch_size)
        x_flat = x.view(B, -1)  # (B, in_channels*patch_size**2)
        x_emb = self.x_embedder(x_flat).unsqueeze(1)  # (B, 1, hidden_size)
        t_emb = self.t_embedder(t)  # (B, hidden_size)
        y_emb = self.y_embedder(y, self.training)  # (B, hidden_size)
        c = t_emb + y_emb  # (B, hidden_size)
        x_feat = x_emb  # (B, 1, hidden_size)
        # dummy grid and mask handling (passed through)
        freqs_cos = torch.ones(B, 1, 1, device=x.device)
        freqs_sin = torch.ones(B, 1, 1, device=x.device)
        global_adaLNm = 0.0
        
        for block in self.blocks:
            x_feat = block(x_feat, c, mask, freqs_cos, freqs_sin, global_adaLNm)
        out = self.final_layer(x_feat, c)  # (B, 1, patch_size**2 * in_channels)
        # reshape the output into image patch shape (B, in_channels, patch_size, patch_size)
        out = out.view(B, self.in_channels, self.patch_size, self.patch_size)
        return out

    def finetune(self, type, unfreeze):
        if type == 'full':
            return
        for name, param in self.named_parameters():
            param.requires_grad = False
        for unf in unfreeze:
            for name, param in self.named_parameters():
                if unf in name:
                    param.requires_grad = True

def split_image_regions(img, patch_size=256, overlap=32):
    """
    Split an image (Tensor CxHxW) into overlapping patches.
    Returns a list of dicts with keys: 'patch' and 'coords' (y,x).
    """
    _, H, W = img.shape
    stride = patch_size - overlap
    regions = []
    for y in range(0, H - patch_size + 1, stride):
        for x in range(0, W - patch_size + 1, stride):
            patch = img[:, y:y+patch_size, x:x+patch_size]
            regions.append({'patch': patch, 'coords': (y, x)})
    return regions

class GatedRegionMerger(nn.Module):
    """
    A simple gated merging module that averages overlapping regions.
    This version collects patches and then forms a full image.
    """
    def __init__(self, in_channels, hidden_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, hidden_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(hidden_channels, in_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
    
    def forward(self, region_results, output_size):
        # region_results: list of tuples (patch_output, (y,x))
        B, C = region_results[0][0].shape[:2]
        H, W = output_size
        accum = torch.zeros(B, C, H, W, device=region_results[0][0].device)
        counts = torch.zeros_like(accum)
        patch_size = region_results[0][0].shape[-1]
        
        for patch_out, coords in region_results:
            y, x = coords
            accum[..., y:y+patch_size, x:x+patch_size] += patch_out
            counts[..., y:y+patch_size, x:x+patch_size] += 1
        merged = accum / counts.clamp(min=1.)
        # Optionally pass through a conv net to act as a gate (here, a simple nonlinearity)
        gated = F.relu(self.conv2(F.relu(self.conv1(merged))))
        return gated

def region_based_pipeline(image, model, patch_size=256, overlap=32, device="cpu"):
    """
    Process a high-resolution image in overlapping regions:
     • Splits image.
     • Processes each patch through the model.
     • Merges results with a gated region merger.
    """
    print("\n[Experiment 1] Starting region-based pipeline...")
    regions = split_image_regions(image, patch_size, overlap)
    region_results = []
    for reg in regions:
        patch = reg['patch'].to(device)  # (C, patch_size, patch_size)
        patch = patch.unsqueeze(0)       # add batch dimension -> (1, C, patch_size, patch_size)
        # Create dummy diffusion timestep and dummy label (for our dummy model)
        t = torch.tensor([0.5], device=device)
        y = torch.tensor([1], device=device, dtype=torch.long)
        # Create dummy grid and mask (not used in dummy version)
        grid = torch.zeros(1, 2, 1, device=device)
        mask = torch.ones(1, 1, device=device)
        # Forward pass
        out = model.forward(patch, t, y, grid, mask, size=patch.shape[-2:])
        region_results.append((out, reg['coords']))
        print(f"Processed patch at coords {reg['coords']}")
    # Merge predictions back into a full image using gated merging:
    merger = GatedRegionMerger(in_channels=region_results[0][0].shape[1], hidden_channels=64).to(device)
    full_result = merger(region_results, output_size=image.shape[-2:])
    print("[Experiment 1] Completed merging of regions.")
    return full_result

Explanation of the Code Structure:

1. Dummy FiT Model:
  • A simplified FiT class and its related embedding/block classes are defined.
  • The forward() method mimics processing an input patch and outputs an image patch.

2. Experiment 1 – Region-Based Pipeline:
  • The function split_image_regions() divides a high-resolution image tensor into overlapping patches.
  • region_based_pipeline() processes each patch via the dummy model (printing patch coordinates) and then merges them using GatedRegionMerger.
  • The merged output image is printed.

3. Experiment 2 – Spot Fine-Tuning:
  • The get_spot_finetune_optimizer() and train_spot_finetune() functions simulate selective parameter updating.
  • A training loss curve is plotted and saved as a PDF named “training_loss_baseline.pdf”.

4. Experiment 3 – Hybrid Pipeline:
  • The training_free_pipeline() runs the region-based processing without fine-tuning.
  • The hybrid_pipeline() first processes the image, then applies a few fine-tuning steps, and processes it again.
  • A dummy evaluation is conducted and the results are plotted and saved as “accuracy_hybrid_vs_text.pdf”.

5. Test Function:
  • The test_code() function sets up a dummy high-resolution image and a few dummy datasets/experiments,
    prints output information and saves plots. This test finishes immediately so that one can quickly verify the code.

All plots are saved as PDF files following the naming convention (for example, “training_loss_baseline.pdf” or “accuracy_hybrid_vs_text.pdf”). 

To run a quick test, simply run the script:
   python experiment.py

This will output printed logs to standard output and save the plots in the current working directory.
